how: A member proposed the European flag and divided its work before others reported joining.
Repeated calls recruited members and national subreddits for building and defending a European flag.
Members accepted plans with bare reports of duty, joining, and work underway.
Proposals selected the European flag, its stars, location, outlines, and later additions.
A common artifact can be built while participants dispute whether it represents Europe, the European Union, or their preferred national identities.
Participants reported construction progress, misplaced stars, continuing work, and completed repairs.
Builders requested and supplied coordinates, pixel plans, layouts, and a manual overlay.
Participants offered scripts, recounted competing automated versions, and argued whether using them was fair.
This room is a documented decided-order case because participants explicitly divided work into equal taskforces and circulated a vote on the flag dispute.
A proposed division or vote establishes deliberate organisation without establishing that every placer accepted it or that the poll settled the dispute.
Plans moved through Discord and national subreddits and returned as work instructions, competing versions, and reports of decisions.
Members defended stars and borders, repaired vandalism, and recalled keeping the original flag alive through attacks.
Keeping work also required budgeting attention around cooldowns, sleep, paid work, and competing ordinary activities.
Participants corrected a mistaken overwriting accusation and separated organised groups from random attackers.
Members refused unwanted overwriting, rejected attacks as petty, and redirected effort toward existing work.
Individual restraint need not stop collective destruction when other placers continue expanding.
Participants negotiated borders, reciprocal defence, territory for help, and the ownership of two border pixels.
Requests for national-flag help received offers, refusals, thanks, and competing priorities.
Participants accepted mutual defence and sought joint European and Nordic work.
Participants carried an Irish border plan and a German Discord request into the host discussion.
Negotiators distinguished organised teams from front-page crowds and reported leadership unable to control all placers.
Disputes about who can commit others also concern prior builders being overwritten under an imposed claim of European unity.
Requests for protection and complaints about imposed territory do not establish a durable host regime deciding which guest works may remain.
Members judged contested space short of manpower and the European flag harder to sustain than national flags.
Repeated repainting prompted proposals to leave the Blue Corner and build at an easier location.
Participants read belonging, European politics, and national history through the flags and their conflicts.
Brexit and national-history grievances supplied rivalries carried into canvas attack talk.
An attack proposal explicitly invoked defeated European flags and filthy brexiteers when naming the British flag as its target.
Moderators staged a separate no-English language, map, and flair joke which members performed and challenged.
Recognising the April Fools licence does not settle whether the joke is experienced as inclusive, hostile, or politically exclusionary.
Moderators redirected canvas posts to a dedicated subreddit and later concentrated retrospective discussion in a final sticky.
Host redirection can coexist with continuing local proposals and moderator recruitment rather than ending canvas participation in the host.
Members celebrated restoration, thanked helpers, and claimed small personal contributions.
Participants marked the end and recounted survival, invasions, losses, and participation.
A participant reported learning about and following a partner country after joint canvas work, while another planned an office-wall display.
After placement ended, a participant defended collective credit and corrected a story attributing random attacks to an organised Discord.
Post-event memory disputes also concern whether cooperative achievement conceals unequal space and the destruction of smaller communities.
Members proposed converting rival flags and admitted making a one-pixel alteration to the British name.
Canvas disputes continued through national taunts, revenge talk, and claims of victory over the void.
A call to build became a workroom receiving progress reports and answers that named the proposed flag.
Starting a mark and calling others can be one posted act rather than two distinct successive stages.
Construction reports immediately included hostile changes and calls to defend the emerging flag.
Defending a border brought a neighbour's request to preserve two leaf pixels and a dispute over the boundary.
Restraint can precede any settled treaty, so border agreement is one route to sparing others rather than a necessary initiating stage.
Scripts addressed unattended upkeep and plan fidelity as well as attack pressure, without necessarily increasing an account's permitted placement rate.
A restoration announcement elicited praise and a participant's claim of a small contribution.
Celebration and retrospective reports coexist, but these concepts do not establish that celebrating caused members to begin preserving the record.
A display plan and reported continuing ties are visible without a passage establishing preservation as their cause.
Judged loss or scarcity can elicit refusal to move and continued defence rather than withdrawal from the spot.
Posting a template does not settle design unless competing placers and established teams accept a common version.
A request to coordinate a new flag received a bare commitment to join.
Defensive pressure can exhaust available help rather than release it, while a safe flag can enable help to other drawings.
A participant explicitly offered help against the void conditional on returning territory to France.
A passage reported two lost European flags and proposed united hands to replace the British flag.
Proposals to overwrite the British flag received direct refusals invoking prior labour, pettiness, and competing defensive needs.
Refusals can also be bare, so a reason is a recurrent form rather than a requirement of an attack call's rejection.
The concepts show a rejected takeover and an alternative to stand ground without establishing that an attack call produced a subsequently agreed border deal.
A takeover proposal elicited an explicit taunt about German conduct and the Empire's strength.
An offer of help against the void was answered by acceptance of a mutual-defence pact.
The host visibly linked removals to an unsustainable posting stream, but no passage attributes the policy to one particular earlier recruitment call.
A shared border solution elicited a report that Discord leadership could not control the larger placing crowd.
Joining flags with hearts or adding a dove makes a peace claim that remains open to rejection rather than settling relations beyond the canvas.
Participants could carry joint placing into curiosity and sports-following without announcing a successor canvas or lasting organisation.
Retain ordinary conversational drift beside the event process because incidental university-ranking arguments do not become canvas organisation merely by occurring in its thread.
Retain platform troubleshooting and image-host jokes as incidental discussion whose presence does not warrant another organising mechanism.
Explain how members make canvas activity legible to newcomers without assuming that receiving an explanation recruits the reader into placing.
Explain national-picture identification and teasing as social use of the canvas that need not build, defend, or recruit for a mark.
An ordinary place photograph and appreciative replies became part of the local language performance when a moderator answered the English-titled post with Nein.
